text.p: The Nigerian unit of Royal Dutch/Shell Group said it was in no hurry to resume oil operations in the politically-volatile Ogoniland in Nigeria but was keen to restore goodwill in the region.

"We are not in a rush at all to go back in. Production levels will be for a long time very low. There has been a lot of damage to facilities," Shell Nigeria managing director Brian Anderson told visiting reporters on Tuesday.
"At a time of budget constraints, we don't feel terribly attracted to going in to spend money to refurbish facilities that have been vandalised," he added.
Shell pulled out of Ogoniland in 1993 following the sabotage of its installations by the Movement for the Survival of Ogoni Peoples (MOSOP).
In November last year, Nigeria's military government hanged author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other MOSOP minority rights activists.

MOSOP was campaigning for self-determination for the 500,000-strong Ogoni population and for compensation from Shell for environmental damage to the area that it says the company's oil activities in the area has done.
"We want to go back and try to solve those problems that have been created in Ogoniland," Anderson said.
Shell officials met earlier this year with local Ogoni chiefs and youth groups but has not yet spoken with MOSOP.
The company offered to talk to the Ogonis in May about cleaning up the region but MOSOP rejected it as a publicity exercise.

"It is our intention to restore goodwill to enable us to go back into Ogoniland with first priority of cleaning up the areas and making facilities safe," said Victor Dania, public and community affairs manager for Shell's eastern Nigeria division which covers Ogoniland.
"Resuming production would take some time because a lot of the facilities have been seriously damaged," he told the visiting reporters in Port Harcourt, eastern Nigeria.
Shell output in Ogoniland when the company abandoned operations was running below 30,000 barrels per day (bpd), down from 100,000 bpd at its peak in 1973.
The company produces almost half of Nigeria's two million bpd of crude in a joint venture with state oil company NNPC.
